ambiguous.item: A private key held in your laptop's TPM chip
ambiguous.why: A private key is a secret value, and secrets are normally the 'know' factor; ISC2 doctrine puts it under 'have' only because the TPM makes it a non-exportable hardware-bound credential the user never learns or types. A candidate reasoning from 'it is a secret' lands in the wrong bucket defensibly.

ambiguous.item: You report a peer who is selling leaked ISC2 exam questions to candidates
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Selling stolen exam content is dishonest and unlawful, so reporting it reads as honourable/legal conduct under Canon II; it is scored Canon IV because the harm is to the certification and the profession's standing, and Canon IV carries the duty not to associate with or shelter unethical practitioners.

ambiguous.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
ambiguous.alternative: Canon III — provide diligent and competent service to principals
ambiguous.why: The pressure comes from a principal, so it can be framed as the limit on what a principal may demand (Canon III). Canon II governs because the operative act is refusing to make a dishonest attestation; canon precedence also puts II above III.

ambiguous.item: You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: Disclosing your limits is plain honesty (Canon II). It is scored Canon III because ISC2 treats 'do not claim or take on work you are not competent to perform' as the competence duty owed to principals.

compound.item: You report a vulnerability in a city's emergency dispatch system instead of saving it for a conference talk
compound.why: The stem couples two behaviours resolving to different canons: disclosing a flaw in public-safety infrastructure (Canon I) and forgoing personal/professional glory from a conference disclosure, which is the profession-and-reputation frame of Canon IV. A candidate anchoring on the second half can justify Canon IV.
